sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Break the big word into pieces like snapping apart building blocks. 'Encephal/o' is the brain block, and '-itis' is the block that always means 'red, hot, swollen inflammation.' Put them together and you get 'the brain is inflamed.' Whenever you see '-itis' on the end, something is inflamed.

### Question 2

Think of '-plegia' as the 'frozen still' ending. If a body part has '-plegia,' it cannot move at all, like a statue. Its weaker cousin is '-paresis,' which means only partly weak, not fully frozen.

### Question 3

The word 'musculoskeletal' glues two ideas together: muscles and skeleton. It is the team name for everything that lets you stand up and move. Bones give the frame, and muscles pull that frame around, so the two combining forms name the framework-plus-movers system.

### Question 4

'Quadri-' is the same 'quad' as in a four-wheeler, so four limbs are stuck. 'Para-' points to the lower half, so just the legs are stuck. The front of the word tells you how much of the body the paralysis covers.

### Question 5

Imagine a dimmer switch for a light. '-paresis' is the light turned down low but still glowing a little, so there is some weak movement. '-plegia' is the light switched fully off, so no movement at all. Same body part, different amount of 'off.'

### Question 6

Picture a bone as a crunchy cracker. Osteoporosis is the cracker full of little holes so it crumbles easily, while osteomalacia is the cracker gone soggy and bendy. The endings tell you which problem the bone has: porous and holey versus soft.

### Question 7

Some words are like the word 'bat,' which can be an animal or a baseball bat depending on the sentence. 'Myel/o' is like that: sometimes it means spinal cord and sometimes bone marrow. You look at the rest of the word to decide which one it is.

### Question 8

Snap the word apart: 'arthr/o' is the joint block and '-algia' is the 'ouch, it hurts' block. So arthralgia is simply a hurting joint. It does not promise the joint is swollen or being fixed, just that it aches.

### Question 9

The ending '-tomy' means 'make a cut,' like opening a door to get inside. 'Crani/o' is the skull, so a craniotomy is cutting open the skull to reach the brain, then usually closing it back up. Compare that to '-ectomy,' which means taking something out for good.

### Question 10

The ending '-plasty' is the 'fix it or rebuild it' ending, related to 'plastic,' which can be molded into a new shape. Put it on 'arthr/o' (joint) and you get rebuilding a worn-out joint, such as giving someone a new hip. Each different ending is a different job done to the joint.

### Question 11

Stack the blocks: 'poly-' means many, 'neur/o' means nerve, and '-pathy' means something is wrong or sick. Together they say 'lots of nerves are sick.' The '-pathy' ending is a general 'something's wrong' word, not the fiery '-itis' inflammation word.

### Question 12

Both words start with 'electro' (electricity) and end with '-graphy' (making a recording), like two songs with the same opening and closing notes. The middle word tells you the instrument: 'my/o' is muscle, 'encephal/o' is brain. So one records muscle signals and the other records brain signals.
